paragraphs: Concept bottleneck models make predictions through an intermediate set of high-level concepts. This gives domain experts a place to correct the model: they can edit mistaken concept predictions before the final answer is produced. The paper studies how to choose those edits, asking how much the intervention procedure itself affects the benefit of human input.

The authors develop several strategies for selecting concepts to intervene on and examine their behavior across different circumstances. Their evaluations include real datasets and synthetic datasets generated from different causal graphs. These tests explore how intervention effectiveness changes with the relationships underlying the data and with the granularity at which corrections are made.

In realistic settings, an informed strategy can reduce task error more than ten times compared with the current baseline using the same number of interventions. That benefit varies substantially with intervention granularity. The authors also identify pitfalls that raise reliability and fairness concerns, showing that providing an editable concept layer alone does not settle how interventions should be used.
icml-2023-a-closer-look-at-the-intervent.tldr: Choosing which concepts to correct can dramatically improve concept bottleneck models, but intervention granularity and procedural pitfalls affect the benefit.

paragraphs: Safety in reinforcement learning can mean limiting accumulated costs, but that does not necessarily prevent an unsafe action or state at a particular moment. This paper addresses the stricter requirement that hard safety constraints hold at every step. Its setting includes both unsafe states and unsafe actions, so safety must cover where the learner goes as well as what it does.

The authors develop a near-optimal algorithm for episodic Markov decision processes under a linear mixture model. Within this setting, the algorithm remains safe at each step while controlling regret, the performance lost during learning. Its regret bound depends on the feature dimension, episode length, number of episodes, and a safety-related parameter.

The upper bound nearly matches existing regret results for settings with only unsafe actions and for unconstrained learning. A complementary lower bound shows that dependence on the safety parameter is unavoidable. This supports the significance of the result without claiming that every factor in the upper bound is exactly optimal.
icml-2023-a-near-optimal-algorithm-for-s.tldr: A theoretically near-optimal reinforcement learning algorithm maintains step-by-step safety with unsafe states and actions under a linear mixture model.

paragraphs: When unobserved confounders prevent a causal query from being identified, the available information may still constrain its possible values. This paper studies how to compute those bounds for quasi-Markovian graphs with discrete observed variables. Existing formulations use multilinear optimization, which can become difficult for solvers when the polynomial objective has degree greater than two.

The main contribution is an equivalent optimization formulation with a lower-degree objective. Its degree depends only on the number of C-components affected by the intervention, rather than the total number of these components in the graph. This ties the complexity of the objective more closely to the particular causal query being asked.

The reformulation enables exact bounds for substantially larger problems than existing techniques can handle. The authors also introduce an efficient Frank-Wolfe heuristic that produces high-quality bounds for large, higher-degree problems. These are two distinct computational contributions: an equivalent formulation that supports exact calculation and a scalable heuristic whose reported quality should not be confused with an exactness guarantee.
icml-2023-causal-bounds-in-quasi-markovi.tldr: An equivalent lower-degree optimization formulation makes exact causal bounds tractable for larger problems with unobserved confounding.

paragraphs: CLIP can recognize images using language with impressive zero-shot ability, but adapting it to a downstream task can weaken performance when test data differ from training data. CLIPood addresses this adaptation problem. It considers unseen test conditions involving domain shifts as well as open classes, where the test setting can include classes beyond those used for adaptation.

The method combines a training objective with an optimization strategy. Margin metric softmax uses class-dependent margins to incorporate semantic relationships supplied by the text modality. Beta moving average maintains a temporal ensemble with weights determined by a Beta distribution, bringing together information from the pretrained zero-shot model and the model adapting to the task.

Experiments across diverse datasets and out-of-distribution scenarios show consistent improvements over the generalization techniques evaluated. The two components address complementary aspects of adaptation: how class relationships guide training and how model information is retained over time. The reported findings support this combination as a way to improve downstream generalization under the tested distribution shifts.
icml-2023-clipood-generalizing-clip-to-o.tldr: CLIPood combines text-informed class margins and temporal model averaging to improve CLIP adaptation under domain shifts and open classes.

paragraphs: Time-series labels are often scarce because annotation is expensive. Consistency regularization helps use unlabeled data by encouraging related versions of an example to receive compatible predictions. This paper develops a version that explicitly uses the sequential structure of the data, making the surrounding observations part of how training examples are constructed.

The proposed context-attached augmentation keeps the target instance intact and attaches preceding and succeeding instances. Different surrounding contexts create different augmented versions of the same target. The framework then shares common labels across these windows using a reliability-based procedure, encouraging consistency when the target appears with different neighboring observations.

This approach changes what varies during augmentation: the context changes while the target itself remains fixed. That gives the learning procedure a way to exploit neighboring information without directly perturbing the target's attributes. Experiments on real-world time-series datasets show that the framework outperforms the existing state-of-the-art consistency regularization methods evaluated, supporting the usefulness of this contextual approach to sparse labels.
icml-2023-context-consistency-regulariza.tldr: Varying the context around an unchanged time-series instance improves consistency-based learning when labels are sparse.

paragraphs: Graph transformers offer a flexible way to learn from graphs, but scaling them to large inputs while retaining competitive accuracy remains challenging. Exphormer addresses this through sparse attention. Its aim is to support powerful graph representations while keeping computational complexity linear in the size of the graph.

The attention structure combines virtual global nodes with expander graphs. Expander graphs provide sparsity alongside mathematical properties such as spectral expansion and pseudorandomness. The authors use these properties to establish theoretical results for the resulting transformer models. This makes the choice of sparse connections part of the mathematical design, rather than simply a reduction in the number of attention operations.

The authors incorporate Exphormer into GraphGPS and obtain competitive results across a broad collection of graph datasets, including state-of-the-art results on three. They also demonstrate operation on larger graphs than those shown in previous graph transformer architectures. Together, these findings indicate that the proposed sparse attention structure can improve scalability while preserving strong accuracy on the evaluated tasks.
icml-2023-exphormer-sparse-transformers-.tldr: Exphormer uses expander graphs and virtual global nodes to give graph transformers linear complexity and competitive empirical accuracy.

paragraphs: Motion forecasting models can struggle when the environment differs from the one represented in their training data. Generative Causal Representation Learning addresses this by modeling features shared across environments separately from features specific to each environment. The goal is to transfer useful knowledge when the distribution of observations changes.

The causal model uses selection variables to identify which parts can transfer directly to a new environment without fine-tuning. An end-to-end variational learning procedure learns the mechanisms that generate observations from the features. The authors also provide theoretical results implying that the causal model is identifiable under certain assumptions; that conclusion is conditional on those assumptions.

Evaluations on synthetic and real-world motion forecasting datasets show substantial improvements over prior models for out-of-distribution prediction in zero-shot and low-shot settings. These findings support the proposed separation of shared and environment-specific factors as a useful basis for transfer. Although the framework is presented as applicable beyond motion forecasting, the reported evaluations concern human trajectory prediction.
icml-2023-generative-causal-representati.tldr: GCRL separates shared and environment-specific causal factors to improve motion forecasting under distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Neural tangent kernel theory studies neural networks through a first-order approximation around their initial weights. This helps explain very wide networks, but the approximation becomes less suitable for narrower networks whose weights move more during training. This paper seeks a mathematical description that extends beyond that linear approximation.

The authors construct an exact power-series representation within a finite neighborhood of the initial weights. It expresses the network using two feature maps, one for data and one for weight changes, and connects training to a reproducing kernel Banach space. This provides a different functional framework from the Hilbert-space treatment associated with neural tangent kernels.

They prove that gradient descent's training sequence can be reproduced exactly by regularized sequential learning in this framework, regardless of network width. The finite-neighborhood setting remains part of the construction. They then derive a uniform convergence bound in which the learning rate and number of iterations play central roles, connecting training choices to a theoretical account of generalization.
icml-2023-gradient-descent-in-neural-net.tldr: An exact local power-series representation connects neural-network gradient descent at any width to sequential learning in a Banach space.

paragraphs: Learning-augmented algorithms use machine-learning predictions as additional input while retaining rigorous performance guarantees. This paper studies that combination for the multi-option ski rental problem, a problem in online optimization where decisions must be made without complete knowledge of the future. Previously known algorithms for this setting were deterministic, both with and without prediction assistance.

The authors develop the first randomized learning-augmented algorithm for the problem. Its construction builds on a new randomized competitive algorithm whose guarantee is proved best possible. Randomization therefore supplies the foundation for improving the prediction-assisted method, rather than being introduced only as an experimental variation.

The resulting learning-augmented guarantees surpass those of prior deterministic algorithms. The paper also supplies lower bounds for deterministic and randomized approaches, helping establish the limits against which these guarantees should be judged. Computational experiments evaluate the performance improvements. Together, the theoretical bounds and experiments show how prediction assistance and randomization can be combined in this particular online decision problem.
icml-2023-improved-learning-augmented-al.tldr: A randomized prediction-assisted algorithm improves guarantees for multi-option ski rental using a best-possible randomized competitive algorithm.

paragraphs: Decentralized federated learning removes the central server and lets clients exchange information only with neighboring clients. However, their local models can become inconsistent, especially when clients have different data distributions or communication links are sparse. The paper targets this inconsistency as a source of poorer performance compared with centralized federated learning.

DFedSAM uses Sharpness Aware Minimization to find local models with low loss across nearby parameter settings. Its gradient perturbations encourage flatter solutions. DFedSAM-MGS adds multiple gossip steps, increasing the mixing of these local models across the communication network. This additional communication is intended to improve agreement while balancing communication cost and generalization.

The authors derive improved convergence rates for both algorithms in a nonconvex setting. The bounds explicitly depend on the communication network's spectral gap, and the second also incorporates the number of gossip steps. Empirically, the methods outperform existing decentralized approaches and can compete with centralized ones. The results connect local optimization choices and network communication to better model consistency.
icml-2023-improving-the-model-consistenc.tldr: Flatter local models and additional gossip steps improve model agreement, convergence, and empirical performance in decentralized federated learning.

paragraphs: Temperature scaling changes how sharply a model concentrates probability on its preferred outputs. In autoregressive generation, the usual procedure applies this adjustment to the next token at each step. The paper argues that this local procedure is myopic and introduces Long Horizon Temperature Scaling to target the temperature-scaled joint distribution of complete samples.

The authors derive a temperature-dependent training objective that optimizes long-horizon sample likelihood. Fine-tuning across a range of temperatures produces a single model whose long-horizon temperature remains controllable during generation. The proposed approach is compatible with likelihood-based models generally, and its evaluation includes both image diffusion models and autoregressive character and language models.

The experiments demonstrate advantages over myopic temperature scaling in likelihood and sample quality, along with a reported 10% accuracy improvement on a multiple-choice analogy task. These findings suggest that controlling the probability distribution over whole outputs can change generation behavior in useful ways. The contribution includes both the joint-distribution objective and a practical method for supporting multiple temperatures within one model.
icml-2023-long-horizon-temperature-scali.tldr: Long Horizon Temperature Scaling trains models to control temperature over complete samples, improving tested likelihood and generation quality.

paragraphs: Speech enhancement can be evaluated using metrics that do not align closely with a model's ordinary training loss. MetricGAN approaches address this discrepancy by making evaluation metrics part of the optimization objective. Optimizing several metrics together introduces another difficulty: their gradient directions can give confusing guidance to the model.

MetricGAN-OKD assigns each of several generators its own target metric. A generator can therefore learn reliably toward one objective while also imitating the other generators through online knowledge distillation. This creates a way to exchange useful behavior across metric-specific models without requiring each generator to learn directly from all metric objectives simultaneously.

Experiments on speech enhancement and listening enhancement show significant improvements across multiple metrics compared with existing multi-metric optimization approaches. The authors explain the strong performance in terms of network generalizability and correlations between metrics. The findings support using specialized generators that learn from one another as a practical approach to managing multiple evaluation objectives in these tasks.
icml-2023-metricgan-okd-multi-metric-opt.tldr: MetricGAN-OKD improves multiple speech-enhancement metrics by letting metric-specific generators learn from one another through online distillation.

paragraphs: People and models can generalize concepts through rules or through similarity to known examples. This paper examines these modes in natural visual data, where concepts vary substantially in complexity. It asks both how visual concepts are represented and how the complexity of those representations relates to different forms of generalization.

Using Representativeness of Attribute, the authors computationally find that models describe concepts using highly representative attributes. They also confirm an inverted-U relationship between visual complexity and description length: description length rises and then falls as visual complexity increases. Separately, they hypothesize that category-conditioned visual modeling could supply a prior by estimating how visual and categorical attributes co-occur.

Experiments show different patterns for the two generalization modes. Representations with relatively high subjective complexity perform better in rule-based generalization, while relatively low-complexity representations perform better in similarity-based generalization. These results suggest that the usefulness of a representation's complexity depends on the generalization procedure, rather than following a single direction across both modes.
icml-2023-on-the-complexity-of-bayesian-.tldr: Representation complexity relates differently to rule-based and similarity-based generalization in natural visual concepts.

paragraphs: Learning a complex task from one demonstration becomes harder when the environment's hidden dynamics change over time. This paper addresses both challenges by representing a task as a sequence of meaningful skills. The framework separates inferring which skills the demonstration contains from producing the actions needed to execute those skills under the current dynamics.

A vision-language model learns a semantic skill set from offline video data, representing skills in a shared vision-language embedding space. From a single demonstration of an unseen task, the system infers a skill sequence. It then combines meta-learning with dynamics inference to adapt skill execution without additional task demonstrations.

Evaluations use extended, multi-stage Meta-world tasks under several one-shot imitation scenarios. The framework performs better than the compared baselines in learning complex tasks, handling dynamics changes, and accommodating different demonstration conditions and modalities. These results support skill composition as a useful bridge between recognizing a demonstrated task and carrying it out when the environment behaves differently.
icml-2023-one-shot-imitation-in-a-non-st.tldr: A vision-language skill framework learns complex tasks from one demonstration and adapts skill execution to changing environmental dynamics.

paragraphs: Event sequences can reveal relationships among event types even when timestamps are unavailable. Neural sequence models can capture complicated historical dependencies, but those dependencies are often difficult to interpret. This paper introduces a probabilistic attention-to-influence model that combines instance-specific interactions with an explicit representation of which event types influence a type of interest.

The framework starts with sequence data and a prior distribution over type-level influence. Through an attention-to-influence transformation and variational inference, it learns an approximate posterior over those relationships. It then samples from this posterior to direct attention toward influencing event types when modeling the conditional likelihood of a sequence.

Experiments on synthetic data and real-world benchmarks show improvements over existing baselines for both prediction and influencing-set identification. The contribution is therefore about making useful predictions and extracting structured information about event relationships within the model. Its probabilistic influence representation provides an interpretable counterpart to the more detailed interactions captured by the neural sequence component.
icml-2023-probabilistic-attention-to-inf.tldr: A probabilistic attention model learns type-level influence relationships while improving prediction from event sequences without timestamps.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning often assumes its dataset comes directly from the task the agent will eventually solve. This paper instead studies multiple datasets collected from randomly perturbed versions of that target task. The setting reflects a distinction between having many observations and having enough different related sources to learn reliably about the target.

An information-theoretic lower bound establishes requirements on both the number of samples and the number of sources. The proposed HetPEVI algorithm explicitly accounts for both uncertainties: limited observations within each source and a limited collection of sources overall. Treating these separately is central to how the method handles heterogeneous data.

The analysis shows that HetPEVI can solve the target task when the sources collectively provide good data coverage. Its optimality guarantee is qualified by a polynomial factor in the horizon length. Extensions to offline Markov games and robust offline reinforcement learning demonstrate that the same design ideas and analysis can apply beyond the initial setting.
icml-2023-provably-efficient-offline-rei.tldr: HetPEVI accounts for both sample and source uncertainty when learning offline from randomly perturbed versions of a target task.

paragraphs: Code completion can depend on information located outside the file being edited. Repo-Level Prompt Generator learns to construct prompts using proposals that draw context from across a repository. These proposals incorporate repository structure and relevant files, such as imports and parent classes, to supply information useful for a particular completion.

The framework operates without access to the code model's weights, making it suitable for black-box models. The experiments study single-line completion using repositories from Google Code archives. An oracle constructed from the prompt proposals achieves a 36% relative improvement over Codex, demonstrating the potential value of selecting suitable repository context.

The authors also train a model to predict which prompt proposal to use and report significant gains over Codex and other baselines. The oracle result and learned-selection result serve different purposes: the first measures the opportunity within the proposals, while the second tests a selection method. Together, they support learning example-specific prompts from repository information.
icml-2023-repository-level-prompt-genera.tldr: Learning to select repository-wide context for prompts improves single-line code completion with black-box language models.

paragraphs: Training normalizing flows through maximum likelihood can require expensive Jacobian determinant calculations. This paper explores a sample-based alternative called the energy objective. Based on proper scoring rules, it avoids determinant calculations during training and supports architectures that are difficult to accommodate within ordinary maximum-likelihood training.

The authors introduce semi-autoregressive energy flows, a model family spanning fully autoregressive and non-autoregressive designs. The alternative objective therefore changes more than the loss function: it permits exploration of a wider range of architectural choices. The study evaluates these flows in terms of sample quality, posterior inference, and generation speed relative to likelihood-trained flows.

Energy flows achieve competitive performance on those measures even though their log-likelihood estimates are generally very poor. The observed performance is decorrelated from likelihood-estimation quality. This finding questions how maximum likelihood should be used as a training objective or evaluation metric in generative modeling, while keeping the claim grounded in the behavior of the studied models.
icml-2023-semi-autoregressive-energy-flo.tldr: A determinant-free energy objective trains flexible normalizing flows with competitive generation despite generally poor log-likelihood estimates.

paragraphs: Sequence models need to capture relevant patterns across long distances without excessive memory, computation, or parameter costs. This paper introduces MultiresLayer, a building block inspired by wavelet-based multiresolution analysis. Its central idea is to capture trends at several scales within the same sequence, rather than relying on a large collection of independent convolution filters.

The core MultiresConv operation uses shared filters arranged in a tree of dilated causal convolutions. This construction combines convolutional computation with the theoretical motivation of wavelet decompositions. The layer requires significantly fewer parameters and has a memory footprint bounded by O(N log N) for a sequence of length N.

Stacking these layers produces state-of-the-art results on several sequence-classification and autoregressive density-estimation tasks involving CIFAR-10, ListOps, and PTB-XL. These findings show that the proposed multiscale structure can support strong predictive performance alongside its resource advantages. The contribution is a reusable sequence-modeling component whose design links scale-sensitive representations to efficient convolutional operations.
icml-2023-sequence-modeling-with-multire.tldr: MultiresLayer uses shared multiscale convolutions to model long sequences efficiently while achieving strong results on several sequence tasks.

paragraphs: An agent learning from images needs a useful representation of its environment. This paper focuses on representations that combine three-dimensional information with semantic and object-centered information. SNeRL learns such a representation from multiple views, aiming to address the weak incorporation of intuitive 3D understanding in previous reinforcement-learning representations.

The method jointly trains a convolutional encoder and semantic-aware neural radiance fields. Alongside the RGB radiance fields, it introduces fields for 3D semantics and distilled features. These parallel components allow the learned implicit representation to include semantic and object-related information together with the visual information represented by the radiance fields.

The reported comparisons show that SNeRL outperforms both earlier pixel-based representations and more recent 3D-aware representations in model-free and model-based reinforcement learning. Those results support enriching a 3D representation with semantic content for the evaluated learning settings. The key contribution is the joint representation-learning design, which brings multiple views, radiance information, semantic fields, and a convolutional encoder into one training approach.
icml-2023-snerl-semantic-aware-neural-ra.tldr: SNeRL combines semantic neural radiance fields and an image encoder to improve representations for model-free and model-based reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Bandit algorithms adapt their choices as they learn, but evaluating a policy also requires quantifying uncertainty about its outcomes. Delayed feedback complicates that evaluation, particularly when delays differ across treatment arms. This paper develops an inference framework that allows the policy being evaluated to differ from the policy that collected the data.

The proposed estimator uses adaptive weights to address two problems at once. It incorporates arm-dependent delays to achieve consistency and controls variance inflation when some choices become increasingly unlikely during data collection. The method does not critically rely on being able to estimate the unknown delay mechanism, an important feature of its design.

Under appropriate conditions, the authors prove that the estimator approaches a normal distribution as the number of time points grows. This provides a basis for large-sample uncertainty statements rather than an unconditional finite-sample guarantee. Monte Carlo experiments illustrate finite-sample behavior. The contribution extends bandit analysis beyond reward maximization to statistical evaluation under delayed and adaptively collected observations.
icml-2023-statistical-inference-on-multi.tldr: An adaptively weighted estimator enables policy evaluation with arm-dependent delayed bandit feedback and conditional large-sample inference guarantees.

paragraphs: When labeled images are scarce, reserving some for validation leaves fewer available for training. This paper investigates whether synthetic images can support model selection instead. The idea gives generated data a different role from the usual practice of adding synthetic examples to the training set.

For image classification, the authors demonstrate that synthetic data can replace a held-out validation set in data-scarce conditions. This makes it possible to train on a larger collection of real examples. Model selection then depends on how well performance measured on generated images reflects performance in the real domain, making the quality of that error estimate central to the approach.

The paper introduces a calibration method to align synthetic error estimates with real-domain errors. This calibration significantly improves the usefulness of synthetic data for selecting models. The findings support synthetic validation as a way to use scarce data more effectively, with calibrated error estimates helping connect evaluation on generated images to the real task.
icml-2023-synthetic-data-for-model-selec.tldr: Calibrated synthetic validation data can support image-classifier selection while freeing scarce real examples for training.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning commonly trains representations by drawing positive pairs together and pushing negative pairs apart. This paper reframes the problem as matching sets of points. That perspective makes the relationships across a collection of examples part of the formulation and provides a route to deriving several contrastive objectives within one framework.

The authors formulate learning as inverse optimal transport with two nested optimization problems. The outer problem learns representations, while the inner problem learns a probabilistic matching matrix between point sets. Relaxing the inner constraints to different degrees produces three contrastive losses. InfoNCE, a widely used contrastive objective, appears as one member of this family.

The soft matching formulation also induces a uniformity penalty related to the uniformity encouraged in contrastive learning. Vision benchmark experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the derived losses and the additional penalty. The result offers both an interpretation of an established objective and a broader design framework for changing matching constraints and representation regularization.
icml-2023-understanding-and-generalizing.tldr: Viewing contrastive learning as inverse optimal transport unifies InfoNCE with additional losses and yields a useful uniformity penalty.

paragraphs: Source separation tries to recover individual signals from observations in which they have been mixed together. Because this problem is ill-posed, it requires prior information about the sources. Learning that information from data can be difficult in planetary missions, where large datasets may be unavailable. This paper develops an unsupervised approach for such limited-data settings.

The method solves an optimization problem in a wavelet scattering covariance representation. This representation is interpretable and low-dimensional for stationary processes, and it captures non-Gaussian statistical properties. Those properties provide useful information for separating signals even when only a small amount of suitable reference data is available.

The authors demonstrate the approach on seismometer recordings from NASA's InSight mission on Mars. They remove transient disturbances caused by thermally induced microtilts, known as glitches, using only a few glitch-free snippets. This real-data example shows how a carefully chosen statistical representation can make source separation possible with a small reference collection in the studied application.
icml-2023-unearthing-insights-into-mars-.tldr: Wavelet scattering covariances enable unsupervised removal of glitches from Mars seismic recordings using only a few glitch-free snippets.

paragraphs: Vision-language transformers process information across multiple modalities, making compression a question of how to distribute reductions across different model components. UPop introduces a unified framework for finding smaller subnetworks within these models. It addresses both where pruning should occur and how the resulting subnetwork should be searched for and retrained.

The unified search operates in a continuous optimization space and automatically assigns pruning ratios among compressible modalities and structures. This lets compression decisions be considered together across the model. The progressive component searches and retrains the subnetwork in stages, maintaining convergence between those activities to attain higher compression ratios.

Experiments across different tasks, datasets, and model architectures demonstrate the framework's effectiveness and versatility. The findings support the combination of coordinated pruning allocation and progressive retraining for vision-language compression. The method's significance lies in treating a multimodal model as a connected compression problem while providing a staged procedure for obtaining and training the smaller network.
icml-2023-upop-unified-and-progressive-p.tldr: UPop compresses vision-language transformers by jointly allocating pruning across components and progressively searching and retraining subnetworks.
